description: How to recognise architectural styles on the street, from Egyptian temples to mass timber: the structural idea that made each possible, what it reacted against, and how to tell look-alikes apart. With a fundamentals subdeck on structure, plans and facade vocabulary.

notes.front: Why does post-and-lintel stone construction end up as a forest of columns?
notes.back: A stone beam fails in tension on its underside as it bends; stone is weak in tension, so spans stay short and columns must stand close together.
notes.analogy: Snap a stick of chalk: it breaks on the stretched side, not the squeezed side. A stone lintel is a chalk stick.
notes.extra: See it: Karnak's hypostyle hall, the Parthenon. Timber and steel beams take tension, so their spans are many times longer.

notes.front: How does a true arch carry load, and what does it demand in return?
notes.back: Wedge-shaped voussoirs press on each other so the whole ring works in compression; in return it pushes outward (thrust) and needs heavy abutments or neighbouring arches.
notes.analogy: A row of people leaning shoulder-to-shoulder in a curve: nobody falls as long as the two at the ends are braced against something.
notes.extra: Pitfall: the keystone is not magic; it is just the last voussoir that closes the ring and lets the centering (timber formwork) come out.

notes.front: A masonry arch is built from stones with no tensile strength. Why does it still stand?
notes.back: Its shape sends the load along a path that is purely compression; each stone is pressed against its neighbours, so no part needs to resist pulling apart.

notes.front: What is thrust, and why does it govern almost all masonry design?
notes.back: The sideways push an arch, vault or dome exerts at its supports. Every masonry style is largely a strategy for absorbing it: thick walls, buttresses, flyers, tie rods, chains.
notes.analogy: 'An arch never sleeps' (old builders' saying): it pushes outward day and night, so something must push back forever.

notes.front: What happens to an arch if its supports spread apart or are not buttressed?
notes.back: The ring loses its compression path: it drops at the crown and cracks at the haunches, then collapses. This is why every arch needs abutments, buttresses or ties.

notes.front: Round arch vs pointed arch: what does the pointed one buy the builder?
notes.back: A semicircle fixes height = half the span and pushes strongly outward. A pointed arch can reach any height for a given span and directs thrust more steeply downward, so supports can be slimmer.
notes.extra: Bonus: in a rectangular bay, pointed arches of different spans can reach the same crown height; semicircles cannot.

notes.front: Why does a semicircular arch fail over a rectangular bay, and what fixes it?
notes.back: A semicircle's height is half its span, so arches of different spans have crowns at different heights. Pointed arches can be struck to any height, so all ribs can meet at one level.

notes.front: Why is a corbelled arch not a true arch?
notes.back: Each course just overhangs the one below (cantilevered steps), so stones work in bending, not compression. It needs mass above to hold the steps down and spans little.
notes.extra: See it: Mycenaean Treasury of Atreus, Maya 'arches'. Triangular profile is the tell.

notes.front: Barrel vault: what is it and what is its structural drawback?
notes.back: An arch extruded into a half-cylinder. Its thrust acts along the whole length of both supporting walls, so the walls must be thick and nearly windowless.
notes.analogy: A long cardboard tube pressed from above: it tries to flatten along its whole length, not at one point.

notes.front: What does a groin vault change compared with a barrel vault?
notes.back: Two barrel vaults intersect at right angles; the thrust gathers along the groins to the four corners. Supports become piers, and the walls between can open up.
notes.analogy: A tent held by four pegs instead of a wall of sandbags along each side.
notes.extra: Limit: with semicircular vaults the bay must be square, or the groins become awkward ellipses.

notes.front: What is a rib vault, and why was it such a leap?
notes.back: A skeleton of stone ribs built first, then thin webs of infill laid between them. Lighter, needs less centering, and with pointed ribs any rectangular bay works.
notes.analogy: An umbrella: the ribs carry the load; the fabric between them only keeps the rain out.
notes.extra: Result: the Gothic cathedral: load runs down ribs to piers, so walls become glass.

notes.front: What is the structural problem of a masonry dome, and how is it solved?
notes.back: Its lower part tries to spread outward (hoop tension) and cracks. Solutions: very thick base (Pantheon), iron chains or tie rings (Florence, St Peter's), or a heavy drum.
notes.analogy: An orange cut in half and pressed down flat: the rim splits. A chain around the rim stops it.

notes.front: Why does a masonry dome crack along meridian lines, and what do chains or tension rings do?
notes.back: The lower part tries to spread outward (hoop tension) and masonry cannot resist pulling, so vertical cracks open. A chain or ring around the base acts like a belt, supplying the missing tension.

notes.front: Pendentive vs squinch: both put a dome on a square room; how do they differ?
notes.back: A pendentive is a curved spherical triangle that smoothly turns square into circle (Byzantine). A squinch is a small arch or niche across each corner, turning square into octagon (Persian, Islamic).
notes.extra: Tell: pendentives look like a continuous sphere cut by four arches; squinches look like corner bridges, often filled with muqarnas.

notes.front: Why does a dome on a square room need pendentives or squinches at all?
notes.back: A circular dome base can only rest on a circle, but the room has four walls and four corners. Pendentives or squinches carry the load from the circle down to the corners.

notes.front: Why does a truss span so far with so little material?
notes.back: It is made of triangles, which cannot change shape without changing a side's length, so loads become pure tension or compression in slender members rather than bending.
notes.analogy: A square picture frame racks into a parallelogram; add one diagonal and it is rigid.
notes.extra: See it: timber roof trusses, iron railway bridges, the Eiffel Tower lattice.

notes.front: Why is a triangle rigid while a square frame is not?
notes.back: A triangle cannot change shape without changing the length of a side, so it holds. A square can shear into a rhombus with no side changing length, so it needs bracing.

notes.front: Why could cantilevers only become dramatic after 1900?
notes.back: A cantilever is held at one end only, so its top is in strong tension. That needs steel or reinforced concrete; masonry can only corbel a little.
notes.extra: See it: Wright's Fallingwater terraces (1937), balconies on any modern tower, stadium roofs.

notes.front: Load-bearing wall vs frame: what is the difference and what follows from it?
notes.back: In a bearing-wall building the walls carry the floors, so they thicken downward and windows stay small. In a frame, columns and beams carry everything; walls are a hung skin, so any facade and any plan become possible.
notes.analogy: Crab vs vertebrate: an exoskeleton you live inside, or an internal skeleton wearing a soft skin.

notes.front: Why did bearing-wall masonry hit a height ceiling around 16 storeys?
notes.back: The walls at the base must grow with every storey added. Chicago's Monadnock Building (1891) needed 1.8 m thick ground-floor walls, eating rentable floor area and light.

notes.text: Material behaviour drives style: stone and brick are strong in {{c1::compression}} only, steel and timber are strong in {{c2::tension}} as well, and reinforced concrete pairs {{c3::concrete (compression) with steel bars (tension)}}.
notes.extra: Consequence: masonry cultures build arches, vaults and domes; tension-capable materials build beams, trusses, cantilevers and frames.

notes.front: Buttress vs flying buttress: what is the difference?
notes.back: A buttress is a mass of masonry thickening a wall where thrust arrives. A flying buttress stands apart and sends thrust to it over a half-arch (the flyer), so the wall itself can stay thin and open.

notes.front: What is centering, and why does it shape what masons could afford to build?
notes.back: The temporary timber formwork that supports an arch or vault until the ring closes. Timber was costly, so forms that reuse centering (repeated bays, ribs first) spread faster.
notes.extra: Example: Brunelleschi's Florence dome was famous partly for needing no centering at all.

notes.front: Pier vs column: what is the difference?
notes.back: A column is a round, usually classical shaft with base and capital. A pier is a massive, often square or compound masonry support, typical of Romanesque and Gothic.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: What made Roman concrete revolutionary compared with cut stone?
notes.back: Volcanic ash (pozzolana) + lime + rubble set hard, even under water, and could be poured into any shape by unskilled labour. Vaults and domes no longer depended on carved voussoirs.
notes.analogy: Liquid stone: pour it into a mould instead of carving it block by block.
notes.extra: Peak: the Pantheon's 43 m dome (AD 126), unmatched until the 19th century. The recipe was lost after Rome and reinvented as Portland cement in 1824.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: What did reinforced concrete add, and when did it arrive?
notes.back: Steel bars inside the concrete take the tension, so one material can bend, cantilever and frame. Patented systems (Hennebique, 1892) made it a general building method by 1900.
notes.analogy: Concrete is bone, steel is tendon: together they handle both squeeze and pull.
notes.extra: Why it matters: it is the material behind Perret, Le Corbusier's Dom-ino frame and all of Brutalism.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.text: 19th-century iron: {{c1::cast iron}} is strong in compression but brittle (columns, 1780s on); {{c2::wrought iron}} takes tension (beams, Eiffel Tower); cheap {{c3::steel}} (Bessemer process, 1856) does both and enabled the skyscraper frame.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: Why was cast iron used for columns but wrought iron for beams?
notes.back: Cast iron is strong in compression but brittle and weak in tension; a column is in compression. A beam bends, so part of it is in tension, which wrought iron (and later steel) can take.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: What is a curtain wall?
notes.back: A non-load-bearing exterior skin (glass, metal, stone panels) hung from the floor slabs of a frame. The structure is behind it; the facade only keeps weather out.
notes.analogy: A raincoat hung on a skeleton: it keeps the weather out and holds nothing up.
notes.extra: Tell: glass runs continuously past floor levels; no thickening toward the ground.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: A curtain wall can be all glass; a load-bearing wall cannot. Why, and what problem does a glass skin bring?
notes.back: A curtain wall carries only its own weight and wind, with the frame carrying the building, so it can be any thin skin. Glass adds solar heat gain and glare, so it needs shading or cooling.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: Where and why did brick rather than stone dominate?
notes.back: Wherever good stone was scarce but clay plentiful: Mesopotamia, Rome's concrete facings, the Netherlands and north German 'Brick Gothic', Victorian Britain. Brick is small, modular and kiln-made anywhere.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: How do you recognise half-timbered construction, and what is it structurally?
notes.back: A visible timber frame with the panels between filled with wattle-and-daub or brick. The frame carries the load; the infill does not. Upper storeys often jetty (overhang).

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: What is the basilica plan, and where did the church get it?
notes.back: A long rectangular hall: a tall central nave lit by clerestory windows, lower aisles either side, an apse at the end. Borrowed from the Roman law court / market hall.
notes.extra: Why: after 313 Christians needed big halls for congregations; the pagan temple (an exterior shrine) was useless as a model.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: Basilica (longitudinal) vs central plan: what experience does each create?
notes.back: Longitudinal: an axis pulls you forward toward the altar (procession). Central: symmetry about a point, usually under a dome, pulls the eye upward (contemplation, commemoration).
notes.extra: Tension: Renaissance architects loved the central plan as 'perfect'; the clergy kept demanding naves for liturgy. St Peter's got both.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: Latin cross vs Greek cross plan: how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: Latin cross: one long arm (nave) and a shorter transept near the far end: Western medieval churches. Greek cross: four equal arms: Byzantine and Renaissance central-plan churches.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.text: Church plan vocabulary: the {{c1::nave}} is the main congregational hall, the {{c2::transept}} is the cross-arm, the {{c3::crossing}} is where they meet (often under a tower or dome), the {{c4::apse}} is the semicircular end behind the altar.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: What is a clerestory?
notes.back: The upper part of a wall that rises above adjacent roofs and carries windows, lighting the central space from high up. Egyptian halls, basilicas, Gothic naves, factories.
notes.analogy: A lighthouse lantern: windows raised above the neighbouring roofs so light gets in over them.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.text: A classical entablature (the beam the columns carry) has three bands: the {{c1::architrave}} at the bottom (the actual lintel), the {{c2::frieze}} in the middle (often sculpted), and the projecting {{c3::cornice}} on top.
notes.extra: Memory: A-F-C bottom-up. Metopes and triglyphs are the Doric frieze's alternating panels.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: What is a pediment, and what should a broken or segmental one tell you?
notes.back: The low triangular gable over a classical portico or window. Triangular and whole: classical/Renaissance/Neoclassical. Broken, curved or scrolled: Mannerist or Baroque playfulness.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: Pilaster vs engaged column: how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: Both are decorative columns attached to a wall. A pilaster is flat and rectangular in section; an engaged column is a half- or three-quarter round shaft projecting from the wall.
notes.extra: Meaning: neither carries much load; they let a wall 'speak' the classical orders (Alberti, Palladio).

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: What is a cornice doing, visually and practically?
notes.back: The projecting top edge of a wall or entablature: it throws rain clear of the facade and gives the building a visible 'lid'. Modernism removing it is why flat-roofed boxes look capless.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: Oriel vs bay window: what is the difference?
notes.back: Both project from the facade. A bay window rises from the ground; an oriel is cantilevered or corbelled out from an upper floor and does not touch the ground.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: What is rustication, and which floor usually gets it?
notes.back: Masonry cut with deep joints or rough faces so each block reads as massive. Used on the ground floor of palazzi and banks to express strength, with smoother ashlar above.
notes.extra: Related: quoins are the emphasised corner stones; a string course is the horizontal band marking a floor level.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: What does a colonnade vs an arcade tell you about the structure?
notes.back: A colonnade carries a straight entablature on columns (post-and-lintel, Greek). An arcade carries arches on columns or piers (Roman and everything after). Rome combined them on the Colosseum.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: What is the Hippodamian grid, and why have cities used grids ever since?
notes.back: The orthogonal street plan attributed to Hippodamus of Miletus (5th c. BC). Grids are easy to survey, divide into equal lots and extend, so colonists, Romans and 19th-century America all used them.
notes.extra: Roman version: cardo (N-S) and decumanus (E-W) crossing at the forum; many European old towns still show it.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: What did Haussmann do to Paris (1853-70), and why does it still define the 'European city' image?
notes.back: Cut wide straight boulevards through the medieval fabric, lined with uniform six-storey stone apartment blocks, with sewers, parks and vistas to monuments. It became the template for the dense, walkable, mid-rise city.
notes.extra: Also: troop movement and crowd control were explicit motives; the boulevards were hard to barricade.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: Perimeter block vs tower-in-the-park: what are these two urban forms?
notes.back: Perimeter block: buildings line the street edges around a shared courtyard (Haussmann, Berlin, Amsterdam). Tower-in-the-park: free-standing slabs in open green space, roads separate (Le Corbusier, post-war estates).
notes.extra: Lesson: Jane Jacobs (1961) argued streets with continuous frontage and mixed uses are safer and livelier than open space nobody owns.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: What happens to street life when towers stand in open parkland instead of lining the street?
notes.back: The street loses its edges and active frontages, and the space between buildings has no clear owner or purpose. This fed the criticism of post-war estates built to the Athens Charter.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.front: What was Ebenezer Howard's Garden City (1898), and what did it react against?
notes.back: Self-contained towns of ~30,000 ringed by a green belt, combining town amenities with country air; a reaction to the smoke, crowding and disease of the industrial city. Letchworth, Welwyn; ancestor of every suburb and new town.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::02 Fundamentals: Materials, Plans & Vocabulary
notes.text: Vitruvius' three requirements of good building (1st c. BC): {{c1::firmitas}} (soundness), {{c2::utilitas}} (usefulness) and {{c3::venustas}} (beauty). Every later theory argues about their weighting.
notes.extra: Echo: 'form follows function' tilts to utilitas; Beaux-Arts to venustas; High-tech to firmitas on display.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: Why is Egyptian monumental architecture so massive and column-crowded?
notes.back: Two causes: post-and-lintel in stone forbids wide spans, and the buildings (tombs, temples) were meant to last for eternity, so mass itself was the message.
notes.extra: See it: Karnak hypostyle hall: 134 columns, some 21 m tall, spaced barely wider than their diameter.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.text: Egyptian tomb evolution: the flat-topped mudbrick {{c1::mastaba}} was stacked into Imhotep's {{c2::step pyramid}} for Djoser (c. 2650 BC), then smoothed into the true {{c3::pyramid}} at Giza.
notes.extra: Lesson: a new type usually arrives as a stack of the old one before it finds its own form.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: How do you recognise an Egyptian temple on sight?
notes.back: Sloping (battered) walls, a massive twin-towered pylon gateway, open court, then a dark hypostyle hall, then a small sanctuary: increasingly dark, low and exclusive as you move in.
notes.analogy: A funnel of privilege: anyone in the court, priests in the hall, only pharaoh in the sanctuary.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: What is a ziggurat, and why did Mesopotamia build in mudbrick?
notes.back: A stepped temple platform with a shrine on top, approached by stairs. The alluvial plain had no stone or timber, so sun-dried and kiln-fired brick was the only material; most ziggurats have since melted into mounds.
notes.extra: Contrast: a pyramid is a tomb and is solid; a ziggurat is a stair to a temple.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: Which ancient culture used the true arch and vault long before Rome, and why did it not catch on?
notes.back: Mesopotamia (brick arches, vaulted drains and tombs, from the 3rd millennium BC). Greece ignored it because the temple aesthetic was post-and-lintel; Rome made it the basis of everything.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: What is a Greek temple for, and why does that explain its form?
notes.back: A house for the god's statue, not a hall for worshippers; rituals happened at the altar outside. So all effort went to the exterior: a colonnade all round (peripteral) over a small dark cella.
notes.analogy: A jewel box on a pedestal: the gem is locked inside, but the box is the show.
notes.extra: Later consequence: Christians could not reuse the type and took the basilica instead.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: How do you tell the three Greek orders apart on sight?
notes.back: Look at the capital. Doric: plain cushion, no base, stocky shaft. Ionic: two scroll volutes, slender shaft on a base. Corinthian: a basket of acanthus leaves, slenderest of all.
notes.analogy: Doric is the soldier, Ionic the scholar, Corinthian the dandy (Vitruvius likened them to man, matron and maiden).

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: Doric vs Ionic: beyond the capital, what differs?
notes.back: Doric: no base, 20 sharp flutes, triglyph-and-metope frieze, proportion ~1:5.5 (heavy, mainland). Ionic: moulded base, 24 flutes with flat fillets, continuous frieze, ~1:9 (light, Ionian/Asia Minor).

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: Why did Corinthian become the favourite order of Rome and of later 'grand' architecture?
notes.back: It is the richest and most vertical, reads well from any side (no front/back like Ionic volutes) and signals expense. Rome used it everywhere; Renaissance and Beaux-Arts followed.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: What are the optical refinements of the Parthenon, and why bother?
notes.back: Columns swell slightly (entasis) and lean inward, the stylobate curves upward at the centre, corner columns are thicker. They counter the eye's tendency to see straight lines as sagging or thin.
notes.extra: Lesson: Greek 'perfection' was tuned for perception, not geometry; almost no line on the Parthenon is straight.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: Greek vs Roman temple: how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: Greek: on a low stepped platform, columns all round, approachable from any side. Roman: on a high podium with steps only at the front, deep porch, free columns in front and engaged columns along the cella walls (Maison Carrée).

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: What did the arch let Rome build that Greece could not?
notes.back: Wide spans in compression-only materials: aqueducts, bridges, multi-storey arcaded amphitheatres, vaulted baths and halls. Greek architecture topped out at the width of a stone beam.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: What is the one-line description of the Colosseum's facade, and why is it a lesson?
notes.back: Roman structure (concrete, arcades, vaults) wearing Greek dress: superimposed Doric, Ionic and Corinthian half-columns, one order per storey, doing no structural work.
notes.analogy: Roman engineering in a rented Greek tuxedo.
notes.extra: Lesson: from here on, classical orders are often applied ornament, a theme that Renaissance palazzi and Beaux-Arts banks repeat.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: How did the Romans keep the Pantheon dome (43 m, AD 126) from collapsing?
notes.back: Concrete walls 6 m thick at the base, dome thinning from 6 m to 1.5 m at the top, progressively lighter aggregate (pumice up high), coffers to cut weight, and an open oculus instead of a heavy crown.
notes.analogy: A tapering bowl: thick where the stresses are greatest, eggshell-thin at the top.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: Why is the Pantheon one of the most imitated buildings ever?
notes.back: It is the archetype of the central plan: a perfect sphere would fit inside (height = diameter), lit by one oculus, behind a temple-front porch. Every domed rotunda from Palladio to Jefferson quotes it.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: What is a triumphal arch, and why does it matter beyond Rome?
notes.back: A free-standing ceremonial gateway: one or three arches framed by columns and an inscribed attic. Alberti turned the motif into church facades (Sant'Andrea); Napoleon and every capital city revived it.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: What was the Roman basilica, and why did it outlive the temple?
notes.back: A large roofed hall for courts and business: nave, aisles, clerestory, apse for the magistrate. Christianity adopted it wholesale for congregations, so it became the ancestor of every Western church.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::03 Ancient: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome
notes.front: What is opus caementicium faced with brick, and why does it matter for reading Roman ruins?
notes.back: Roman concrete cores with brick or stone facings (opus reticulatum, opus latericium). Ruins show the rubble core because the marble veneer was stripped; the 'brick' Rome you see was once clad.

notes.front: What is the defining structural idea of Byzantine architecture?
notes.back: A great dome over a square space, carried on four arches and pendentives, so the dome needs only four piers and the space below flows freely.
notes.extra: Anchor: Hagia Sophia, Constantinople (532-537), 31 m dome 'hung from heaven by a chain' (Procopius).

notes.front: How do you recognise a Byzantine church on sight?
notes.back: Outside: plain brick, clustered shallow domes, little ornament. Inside: gold mosaics, marble veneer, light from a ring of windows at the dome's base, Greek-cross plan.
notes.analogy: A geode: dull on the outside, glittering within. The opposite of a Greek temple, where all the art is outside.
notes.extra: Also: St Mark's Venice; Byzantine survives in Orthodox church design and in Ottoman mosques (via Hagia Sophia).

notes.front: Why did Romanesque builders (c. 1000-1150) switch from timber roofs to stone vaults?
notes.back: Timber churches kept burning down, and stone vaults had better acoustics and sounded 'eternal'. But stone vaults push outward, so walls became enormously thick and windows tiny.

notes.front: How do you recognise Romanesque on sight?
notes.back: Round arches everywhere, thick walls, small deep-set windows, massive piers, barrel or groin vaults, blind arcading, often twin west towers: fortress-like solidity.
notes.analogy: A castle that became a church: built as if the vault were an enemy pushing the walls out.
notes.extra: Anchors: Speyer, Durham (early rib vaults), Pisa, Cluny (destroyed), Santiago de Compostela. English name: Norman.

notes.front: Why did pilgrimage churches add an ambulatory with radiating chapels?
notes.back: Crowds needed to circulate past relics without disturbing the monks' choir. An aisle wrapping around the apse, with chapels off it, lets pilgrims flow continuously.
notes.analogy: A ring road around the city centre with lay-bys.

notes.front: Where and why did Gothic begin?
notes.back: Abbot Suger's rebuilding of Saint-Denis near Paris (1140-44). He wanted the choir flooded with light as a theology of God-as-light; the pointed arch, rib vault and buttressing were combined to get it.
notes.extra: Note: each element existed before (pointed arches in Islam and Burgundy, rib vaults at Durham); Gothic is the system that uses them together.

notes.front: Name the three parts of the Gothic structural system and the job each does.
notes.back: Pointed arch: height independent of span, steeper thrust. Rib vault: gathers the roof load onto points. Flying buttress: carries the thrust outside the wall.

notes.front: Explain the chain of logic by which Gothic cathedrals got walls of glass.
notes.back: Rib vaults concentrate the roof load and thrust at points (the piers). Flying buttresses carry the thrust from those points outside the building. The wall between piers now carries nothing, so it can be opened into windows.
notes.analogy: Once the tent poles and guy ropes hold the roof, the canvas walls can be unzipped.

notes.front: What would happen to a Gothic nave if its flying buttresses were removed?
notes.back: The vault's outward thrust acts on the thin clerestory wall at the top of the nave with nothing to resist it. The wall bows outward and the vault collapses.

notes.front: What does a flying buttress look like, and what is it doing?
notes.back: A half-arch leaping from an outer pier to the upper nave wall, exactly where the vault lands. It props the wall against the vault's outward push and carries it down the outer pier to the ground.
notes.analogy: A crutch planted outside the body, taking the lean so the body itself can stay thin.

notes.front: Why do Gothic buttresses carry pinnacles?
notes.back: Not just decoration: their weight presses the buttress pier down, steering the diagonal thrust from the flyer more vertically so the pier does not overturn.
notes.analogy: Standing on a ladder's foot while someone leans on it.

notes.front: How do you recognise Gothic on sight?
notes.back: Pointed arches, rib vaults, flying buttresses, stone tracery in huge windows, rose windows, pinnacles and spires, stained glass, relentless verticality; walls look thin and perforated.
notes.extra: Anchors: Chartres, Notre-Dame, Amiens, Reims; Cologne; Salisbury; Milan.

notes.text: A Gothic nave elevation stacks three storeys: the {{c1::arcade}} (arches to the aisles), the {{c2::triforium}} (narrow passage over the aisle roof), and the {{c3::clerestory}} (big windows at the top).

notes.front: In a Gothic nave elevation, which storey admits the most light, and why can it be so large?
notes.back: The clerestory, at the top. The rib vault and flying buttresses carry the roof load and thrust to the piers, so the wall between them carries almost nothing and can be mostly glass.

notes.front: Romanesque vs Gothic: the fastest way to tell them apart?
notes.back: Arches: round = Romanesque, pointed = Gothic. Then walls: thick and solid with small windows = Romanesque; thin and glassy with external buttresses = Gothic.
notes.analogy: Romanesque is a bunker; Gothic is a birdcage of light.

notes.text: Gothic phases by window tracery: {{c1::Early}} (lancets, plate tracery, c. 1140-1200), {{c2::High/Rayonnant}} (bar tracery, radiating rose windows, 1200-1350), {{c3::Flamboyant}} (flame-shaped curves, 1350-1500); England's late variant is {{c4::Perpendicular}} (grid tracery, fan vaults).

notes.front: What happened at Beauvais in 1284, and what is the lesson?
notes.back: The highest Gothic choir vault (48 m) collapsed twelve years after completion. Gothic had reached the limit of masonry; builders had no theory of structure, only trial, error and rules of thumb.

notes.front: Where does the word 'Gothic' come from, and what does that tell you?
notes.back: A Renaissance insult (Vasari): 'barbaric' architecture of the Goths, as opposed to good Roman classicism. Every style name is partly a verdict by whoever came next.
notes.extra: Likewise: 'Baroque' meant a misshapen pearl; 'Brutalism' stuck because it sounded brutal.

notes.front: What is a gargoyle structurally?
notes.back: A carved water spout projecting from a gutter so rain is thrown clear of the wall and foundations. Decoration followed function; grotesques without a spout are not gargoyles.

notes.front: What is tracery?
notes.back: The stone framework subdividing a large Gothic window into panels for glass. Its pattern (lancets, circles, flame curves, grids) is the best clue to date and region.

notes.front: Why do Italian Gothic churches look so different from French ones?
notes.back: Italy never gave up the Romanesque/classical sense of wall and horizontal proportion: wide naves, small windows (strong sun), polychrome marble facades, few flying buttresses. Milan is the exception that proves it.
notes.extra: Anchors: Siena, Orvieto, Florence's Santa Croce.

notes.front: What is a Gothic hall church (Hallenkirche)?
notes.back: Nave and aisles of equal height under one roof, so there is no clerestory and the light comes from tall aisle windows. Common in Germany and Poland; interior feels like a forest, not a canyon.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.text: Mosque vocabulary: the {{c1::qibla}} wall faces Mecca and holds the {{c2::mihrab}} (niche); the {{c3::minaret}} is the tower for the call to prayer; the {{c4::sahn}} is the courtyard, usually with a fountain for ablutions.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: Hypostyle vs domed mosque: the two basic types and where each comes from?
notes.back: Hypostyle: a broad low hall of many columns beside a courtyard, from the Prophet's house (Córdoba, Kairouan). Domed: one great centralised dome over the prayer hall, developed by the Ottomans from Hagia Sophia (Sinan's Süleymaniye).

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: How do you recognise a horseshoe arch, and where does it point you?
notes.back: The curve continues past the semicircle and pinches inward before meeting the impost. Umayyad Spain and the Maghreb: Córdoba's Great Mosque, Moorish and later Neo-Moorish buildings.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: What is muqarnas, and what job does it do?
notes.back: A honeycomb of tiny stacked niches that dissolves a transition: squinches under a dome, the inside of a portal hood, a capital. It turns a structural corner into a stalactite ceiling of light and shadow.
notes.analogy: Fractal corbelling: the awkward join between square and dome is hidden by making it infinitely small.
notes.extra: Anchors: Alhambra's Hall of the Two Sisters; Isfahan's portals.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: Why is the courtyard house the default in Islamic (and most hot-climate) cities?
notes.back: Privacy: blank street walls, life faces inward. Climate: shaded court, fountain and thick walls cool the air; rooms open to the court, not the dusty street. Also allows dense, car-free fabric.
notes.analogy: A house turned inside out: the garden is the living room and the street sees only a wall.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: What is an iwan, and what is the four-iwan plan?
notes.back: A vaulted hall open on one side, framed by a tall rectangular portal. Persian mosques and madrasas place one on each side of the courtyard (four-iwan plan): Isfahan's Friday Mosque.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: Why does Islamic ornament consist of geometry, arabesque and calligraphy?
notes.back: Religious reluctance to depict living beings in sacred settings pushed creativity into infinite geometric patterns, stylised plant scrolls and the written word itself, usually in tile, stucco or carved stone.
notes.extra: Tell: ornament covers surfaces completely but never the structure's logic; arches and domes stay legible.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: Islamic pointed arches predate Gothic by about two centuries. What is the lesson for 'who invented it'?
notes.back: Elements travel (through Sicily, Spain, the Crusades, Amalfi's trade) but a style is the system that exploits them. Islam used the pointed arch for profile and rhythm; Gothic turned it into a structural engine for height.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: What is the structural principle of a traditional Chinese timber building?
notes.back: A post-and-beam timber frame carries the roof; walls are non-bearing screens. The roof load steps down through dougong bracket sets onto columns resting loosely on stone bases.
notes.analogy: A table with a tablecloth: the legs hold the top; the cloth just hangs.
notes.extra: Modern echo: this is Le Corbusier's 'free facade' two thousand years early.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: Why can a traditional Chinese timber building have walls that open or are replaced without risking collapse?
notes.back: The post-and-beam frame carries the roof, so the walls are non-bearing screens. Doors, windows and infill can be placed anywhere or removed.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: What is a dougong, and what does it tell you about the building?
notes.back: An interlocking set of blocks (dou) and arms (gong) between column and eave beam, spreading the roof load and letting the eaves overhang deeply. Its complexity signalled rank; it also flexes in earthquakes.
notes.analogy: A stack of outstretched hands passing the roof down to the column.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: Why are East Asian roofs curved and heavy?
notes.back: The roof is the building's main expressive element because walls do not carry it. Upturned eaves lift the edge to let light in and throw rain clear; heavy tiles and deep overhangs protect the timber and earthen walls.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: What is a siheyuan (Beijing courtyard house), and what does its plan encode?
notes.back: Single-storey halls around a south-facing walled courtyard on a north-south axis. The principal hall at the north is for elders; wings for sons; gate at the south-east: Confucian hierarchy made spatial.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: What made traditional Japanese timber joinery distinctive?
notes.back: Complex interlocking joints cut so precisely that no nails or glue are needed; they can be disassembled and they move in earthquakes. Carpenters (daiku) rather than architects shaped the tradition.
notes.analogy: Cabinet-making at the scale of a building: dovetails, not nails.
notes.extra: Anchor: Hōryū-ji (7th c.), the oldest timber buildings in the world; Ise Shrine, rebuilt identically every 20 years since the 7th century.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: Why has Japanese architecture been a touchstone for modernists?
notes.back: Its traditional house already had a modular grid (the tatami mat), sliding screens (shoji) giving a free plan, raised floors, exposed natural materials and no applied ornament. Wright, Taut and the Bauhaus all studied it.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: Chinese vs Japanese traditional architecture: how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: Chinese: symmetry, bright red and gold paint, ceramic tile, massive bracket sets, axial courtyards. Japanese: asymmetry, unpainted wood, bark or thatch roofs, lighter structure, integration with a garden, calculated austerity.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: How does a Japanese pagoda survive earthquakes?
notes.back: Each storey is a loosely stacked timber frame that can slide, and a central pillar (shinbashira) hangs or stands free, acting like a tuned damper. Almost no pagoda has fallen to an earthquake in 1,400 years.
notes.extra: Echo: Taipei 101's tuned mass damper is the same idea in steel.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: What is vernacular architecture, and why do architects keep returning to it?
notes.back: Buildings made by local people with local materials and inherited know-how, without architects. It is climate-tested over centuries, so it is the baseline for passive design and regional identity.
notes.analogy: A centuries-long A/B test: every bad idea got weathered out, only the survivors are still standing.
notes.extra: Anchor: Rudofsky's 1964 MoMA show Architecture without Architects.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.text: Vernacular responses to climate: hot-dry regions use thick {{c1::adobe/earth}} walls for thermal mass and small openings; hot-humid regions raise houses on {{c2::stilts}} with wide eaves and open walls for airflow; snowy regions use steep {{c3::pitched roofs}} and compact plans.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: Why does thermal mass suit a desert climate but help little in a hot, humid one?
notes.back: Mass absorbs daytime heat and releases it at night, which works when nights are cool. In humid tropics nights stay warm, so ventilation and light, raised construction work better.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: What is a windcatcher (badgir), and what principle does it use?
notes.back: A tower open to the prevailing wind that funnels air down into the house, often over water or a cool cellar (stack and evaporative cooling). Persian Gulf and Iran; the ancestor of passive ventilation strategies.
notes.analogy: A chimney in reverse: it pulls air down instead of pushing smoke up.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::05 Islamic, East Asian & Vernacular
notes.front: What is a Hindu temple organised around, and what is its skyline tell?
notes.back: A small dark sanctum (garbhagriha) under a towering spire (shikhara in the north, stepped vimana in the south), laid out on a mandala grid; the mass is sculpted stone, not a spanned interior.

notes.front: What did Renaissance architecture react against, and what did it revive?
notes.back: Against Gothic's vertical 'barbarism'; for Roman antiquity: the classical orders used correctly, round arches, domes, and above all proportion derived from Vitruvius and from measuring ruins.
notes.extra: Where/when: Florence from the 1420s (Brunelleschi), then Rome, then Europe by 1550.

notes.front: How did Brunelleschi build the Florence Cathedral dome (1420-36) without centering?
notes.back: A pointed double shell (inner structural, outer weather) with horizontal rings and herringbone brick courses that lock each ring as it rises, so the masonry was self-supporting during construction. Tension rings of stone and iron hold the base.
notes.analogy: Stacking bricks in a spiral so each course is a closed ring: a ring can't fall inward.
notes.extra: Why it matters: the first great dome since the Pantheon, 45 m wide, built by someone trained as a goldsmith; the architect as individual genius starts here.

notes.front: What does the Ospedale degli Innocenti (Brunelleschi, 1419) show that Gothic did not?
notes.back: A modular arcade: each bay is a cube under a hemispherical dome, column height = bay width. Architecture as repeated proportional units rather than accumulated craft.

notes.front: What was Alberti's contribution, in one line?
notes.back: He turned building into theory: De re aedificatoria (1452) defined beauty as a harmony 'to which nothing can be added or taken away', and his facades applied Roman motifs (triumphal arch, temple front, scrolls) to churches.
notes.extra: Anchors: Sant'Andrea Mantua (triumphal-arch facade, barrel-vaulted nave), Santa Maria Novella (scrolls hiding the aisle roofs, copied for 300 years).

notes.front: What did Palladio do that made him the most imitated architect in history?
notes.back: Put the classical temple front on houses, organised villas by simple ratios around a central hall, and published it all in the Four Books (1570), which carried his rules to England, Russia and America.
notes.extra: Anchors: Villa Rotonda (four porticos, central dome), Basilica Vicenza (Palladian window), San Giorgio Maggiore. Heirs: Inigo Jones, Lord Burlington, Jefferson's Monticello.

notes.front: What is a Palladian (Serlian) window?
notes.back: A tripartite opening: a tall arched centre flanked by two narrower flat-topped openings with small entablatures. Instant sign of Palladian or Georgian influence.

notes.front: Why did Renaissance architects believe proportion produced beauty?
notes.back: Pythagorean/musical ratios (1:2, 2:3, 3:4) were thought to govern the cosmos; a room 'tuned' like a chord would please the eye as a chord pleases the ear. The column's diameter became the module for the whole building.
notes.analogy: Tuning a room like a guitar string: lengths in whole-number ratios give a chord, not a buzz.
notes.extra: Later: Le Corbusier's Modulor (1948) is the same faith with the golden section and a 1.83 m man.

notes.front: How do you recognise a Renaissance palazzo on sight?
notes.back: A horizontal, symmetric block: rusticated ground floor, smoother upper floors, string courses marking each level, regular rows of pedimented or arched windows, a heavy crowning cornice, courtyard inside.
notes.extra: Anchors: Palazzo Medici-Riccardi, Palazzo Farnese, Palazzo Rucellai (pilaster orders on the facade).

notes.front: What is Mannerism (c. 1520-1600), and how do you spot it?
notes.back: Classical rules broken deliberately by people who knew them: columns set in niches, triglyphs that 'slip', giant keystones, compressed or stretched proportions. Tension and wit rather than calm.
notes.analogy: Jazz: you can only bend the rules convincingly once you know them cold.
notes.extra: Anchors: Michelangelo's Laurentian Library vestibule; Giulio Romano's Palazzo del Tè.

notes.front: What is a giant order, and who popularised it?
notes.back: Columns or pilasters that run through two or more storeys. Michelangelo used it on the Capitoline palaces to unify a facade; Baroque and Neoclassicism made it the sign of grandeur.

notes.front: How did St Peter's dome (Michelangelo, finished 1590) stay up?
notes.back: Double shell on a high drum, ribbed, with iron chains around the base; still cracked, so more chains were added in the 1740s after the first mathematical analysis of a dome (Poleni).
notes.extra: Lineage: Pantheon → Florence → St Peter's → St Paul's (Wren) → US Capitol.

notes.front: What did Baroque architecture want, and why?
notes.back: To move and persuade: the Counter-Reformation church (and absolutist courts) used drama, scale, curves, light and gold to overwhelm the viewer with emotion and authority. It reacted against Renaissance calm and Protestant plainness.

notes.front: How do you recognise Baroque on sight?
notes.back: Curved or undulating facades, oval plans, broken and scrolled pediments, giant orders, clustered columns, dramatic directed light, illusionistic ceilings, grand axial staircases.
notes.extra: Anchors: Bernini's St Peter's colonnade; Borromini's San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane; Versailles; Wren's St Paul's; Vierzehnheiligen.

notes.front: Bernini vs Borromini: the two Roman Baroque temperaments?
notes.back: Bernini: theatrical, sculptural, grand gestures with classical vocabulary (the embracing colonnade). Borromini: geometric, restless, walls that undulate and plans built from intersecting ovals and triangles (San Carlo, Sant'Ivo).

notes.front: Renaissance vs Baroque: how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: Renaissance: flat facades, straight lines, circle and square, each part legible, calm. Baroque: curves, ovals, parts merged into one dramatic whole, movement, the eye never rests.
notes.analogy: Renaissance is a chord held; Baroque is a crescendo.

notes.front: What is Baroque urbanism?
notes.back: Cities organised by long straight avenues radiating to monuments and obelisks (Sixtus V's Rome, 1585), and palaces commanding axial gardens (Versailles). Power made visible as a vista; later copied by Washington DC and Haussmann.

notes.front: What is Rococo, and what did it react against?
notes.back: A light, playful interior style of 1720-70 France and southern Germany: pastel colours, gilded shell-like curves (rocaille), asymmetry, mirrors, no heavy orders. It reacted against the pompous state Baroque of Louis XIV.
notes.analogy: Whipped cream after a heavy state banquet.
notes.extra: Anchors: Hôtel de Soubise salons (Paris), Amalienburg (Munich), Wieskirche (Bavaria).

notes.front: Baroque vs Rococo: how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: Baroque: heavy, dark, grand, exterior and urban in scale, religious/political persuasion. Rococo: light, pastel, intimate, mostly interiors, asymmetric shell ornament, aristocratic pleasure.
notes.analogy: Baroque is the throne room; Rococo is the boudoir next door.

notes.front: Why does Wren's St Paul's (1675-1710) have a triple dome?
notes.back: Outer timber dome for the skyline, inner masonry dome for the interior, and a hidden brick cone between them carrying the heavy stone lantern. Each shell is shaped for its own job, held by an iron chain.

notes.front: What did Neoclassicism (c. 1750-1850) react against, and what fed it?
notes.back: Against Rococo frivolity and Baroque excess. Fed by Enlightenment reason, the excavations of Herculaneum and Pompeii (1738+), Stuart and Revett's Athens surveys, and Winckelmann's 'noble simplicity and quiet grandeur'.
notes.analogy: The sober morning after Rococo's party.

notes.front: How do you recognise Neoclassical on sight?
notes.back: Severe geometry, plain wall surfaces, correct Greek or Roman orders (often baseless Greek Doric), unbroken pediments, no curves, no gilding; white stone or stucco; dome on a temple front for civic buildings.
notes.extra: Anchors: Panthéon Paris (Soufflot), Brandenburg Gate (Langhans), British Museum (Smirke), Altes Museum (Schinkel), US Capitol, Virginia State Capitol (Jefferson).

notes.front: Greek Revival vs Palladian/Roman classicism: how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: Greek Revival: baseless fluted Doric or Ionic, heavier proportions, no arches or domes, colonnade or portico on a plain box. Palladian: Roman orders on bases, round arches, Serlian windows, villa with dome.

notes.front: What did Boullée and Ledoux propose, and why are they remembered?
notes.back: 'Architecture parlante': buildings whose pure geometric form (sphere, pyramid, cylinder) announces their purpose, at gigantic scale. Mostly unbuilt (Boullée's Newton cenotaph), but ancestors of modernism's abstract volumes.

notes.front: Why did the Gothic Revival (c. 1820-80) arise, and what did it claim?
notes.back: Romantic nationalism (Gothic as native, Christian, medieval) against 'pagan' classicism. Pugin's True Principles (1841) argued Gothic was honest: every feature structural, construction visible, ornament only enriching structure.
notes.extra: Anchors: Houses of Parliament (Barry and Pugin), Cologne Cathedral completed 1880, countless Victorian churches; Viollet-le-Duc in France read Gothic as rational engineering.

notes.front: What was the 19th-century 'Battle of the Styles', and what did it reveal?
notes.back: Classical vs Gothic (and later anything: Egyptian, Moorish, Renaissance) chosen per building type: Gothic for churches, classical for banks. Style had become a costume picked from a catalogue, which is what modernism rebelled against.

notes.front: What was Beaux-Arts architecture?
notes.back: The method of the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris: axial, symmetric plans with a clear hierarchy of spaces, grand stairs, lavish classical sculpture and ornament. The style of opera houses, museums, stations and world's fairs, 1860-1920.
notes.extra: Anchors: Paris Opéra (Garnier), Grand Central Terminal, New York Public Library, Petit Palais.

notes.front: Neoclassicism vs Beaux-Arts: how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: Neoclassicism is austere and archaeologically correct, one order, plain walls. Beaux-Arts is opulent and eclectic: paired columns, sculpture, swags, mansard roofs, Baroque richness on a classical plan.

notes.front: What was the City Beautiful movement?
notes.back: American Beaux-Arts urbanism after the 1893 Chicago World's Fair: monumental civic centres, axes, parks and white classical buildings meant to inspire civic virtue. Washington's Mall plan (1901), Chicago's Burnham Plan (1909).

notes.front: What was significant about the Iron Bridge at Coalbrookdale (1779)?
notes.back: The first structure made of cast iron: a 30 m arch, assembled from cast parts using timber-style joints because nobody yet knew how to design in iron. The material arrived before its vocabulary.

notes.front: Why was the Crystal Palace (Paxton, 1851) a turning point?
notes.back: A 560 m glass-and-iron hall built in six months from standardised prefabricated parts on a 24-foot module, then dismantled and moved. Prefabrication, modularity, speed and transparency: the industrial building fully realised.
notes.analogy: A greenhouse scaled to a cathedral, designed by a gardener.

notes.front: What does Labrouste's Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève (1850) show about 19th-century attitudes to iron?
notes.back: Slender cast-iron columns and arches carry the reading-room roof, but they stand inside a stone Renaissance box. Iron was accepted as engineering, not yet as architecture fit for a facade.
notes.analogy: An iron engine inside a stone car body.

notes.front: Why did artists protest the Eiffel Tower (1889), and why does it matter?
notes.back: Its 300 m wrought-iron lattice, shaped by wind calculation rather than any style, was condemned as a 'useless and monstrous' factory chimney. It showed structure alone could be a monument, which High-tech later made a creed.

notes.front: What is the 19th-century split between engineer and architect?
notes.back: Engineers (Paxton, Eiffel, Roebling) built the era's boldest spans in iron and glass; architects dressed buildings in historical styles. Modernism's founding claim was to reunite them.

notes.front: What was the train shed, and what did it teach?
notes.back: A huge iron-and-glass vault (St Pancras, 1868: 73 m clear span) behind a masonry hotel facade. The same building shows both halves of the century: honest engineering at the back, costume at the front.
notes.analogy: A mullet: business at the front, engineering at the back.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: Why did the skyscraper appear in Chicago in the 1880s?
notes.back: The 1871 fire cleared the centre; land prices in the tight Loop soared; and the technology had just assembled: the steel frame, the safety elevator, fireproofing of iron, the telephone and plumbing pumps.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.text: Two inventions made tall buildings possible: the {{c1::steel skeleton frame}} (Jenney's Home Insurance Building, 1885) removed the height limit of bearing walls, and the {{c2::safety elevator}} (Otis, 1853) removed the limit of stairs, making upper floors the best floors.
notes.analogy: Steel lets you build the ladder; the elevator makes tenants willing to climb it.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: What is a Chicago window, and why does it look like that?
notes.back: A wide tripartite window: a fixed central pane with narrow sash windows either side, filling the whole bay between columns. Possible only because the frame carries the load; it maximises light deep into the office floor.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: What did Louis Sullivan mean by 'form follows function', and how did he shape a tall building?
notes.back: Each use should generate its own form; for the office tower that meant a tripartite composition like a column: shops in the base, identical office floors as a soaring shaft, a crowning cornice (Wainwright Building, 1891).
notes.extra: Irony: Sullivan also covered his buildings in lush organic ornament; 'function' did not mean bare.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: Chicago School vs the eclectic skyscraper (New York, 1900-30): what is the difference?
notes.back: Chicago expressed the grid of the frame on the facade (Reliance, Carson Pirie Scott). New York wrapped frames in historical dress: Woolworth Building's Gothic (1913), Beaux-Arts banks, until Art Deco.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: Why do 1920s-30s New York skyscrapers have stepped setbacks?
notes.back: The 1916 zoning law required towers to step back as they rose so light reached the street. The resulting ziggurat profile became the Art Deco silhouette (Empire State, Chrysler).
notes.analogy: A wedding cake carved by a daylight law.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: A south-facing overhang works in summer and winter. Why does it fail on an east- or west-facing window?
notes.back: Morning and evening sun is low and comes from the side, so it passes under the overhang. East and west windows need vertical fins, screens or trees instead.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: What was Art Nouveau (c. 1890-1910), and what did it react against?
notes.back: A deliberate new style against historicist copying: forms from nature (plant stems, whiplash curves), iron and glass used expressively, total design down to door handles.
notes.extra: Anchors: Horta's Hôtel Tassel (Brussels), Guimard's Paris Métro entrances, Gaudí's Casa Batlló and Sagrada Família (Catalan Modernisme), Otto Wagner's Vienna (geometric Secession variant).

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: How do you recognise Art Nouveau on sight?
notes.back: Sinuous asymmetric curves, plant and insect motifs, exposed curling ironwork, stained glass and ceramic tile, windows and doors with organic outlines; the Vienna/Glasgow variant is more rectilinear with gilded geometric ornament.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: Why did Art Nouveau burn out so quickly?
notes.back: Handcrafted total design was expensive and could not be mass-produced; by 1910 it looked like decadent fashion. Loos's 'Ornament and Crime' (1908) and Werkbund industrial logic took over.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: What was the Arts and Crafts movement, and what did it react against?
notes.back: Ruskin and William Morris's revolt against shoddy machine-made goods and the degradation of the worker: honest materials, visible craft, vernacular forms, the medieval guild as model.
notes.analogy: Farmers' market against supermarket, for buildings.
notes.extra: Anchors: Red House (Webb for Morris, 1859), Voysey's houses, Greene & Greene's Gamble House (Pasadena, 1908).

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: How do you recognise Arts and Crafts on sight?
notes.back: Steep roofs, exposed timber, local brick or stone, casement windows in bands, asymmetric vernacular massing, hand-finished joinery and metalwork; the look of a very good farmhouse.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: Arts and Crafts vs Art Nouveau: how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: Both prized craft and nature, but Arts and Crafts is rustic, rectilinear and medieval-vernacular (England, US). Art Nouveau is urban, curvilinear and wilfully new (Brussels, Paris, Barcelona).

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: What is the paradox linking Arts and Crafts to the Bauhaus?
notes.back: The Bauhaus inherited its ideals (truth to materials, unity of arts and crafts, design for everyday life) but reversed the verdict on the machine: Gropius wanted craft quality through industry, not against it.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: What did Adolf Loos mean by 'Ornament and Crime' (1908)?
notes.back: Applied ornament wastes labour and material and goes out of fashion, so it is economically and culturally backward; cultural progress is the removal of ornament from useful objects. A manifesto modernism took literally.
notes.analogy: Loos's own image: ornament is the tattoo, and the tattooed modern man is a criminal or a degenerate.
notes.extra: Anchor: Looshaus, Vienna (1910): plain upper floors scandalised the city.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: What was Art Deco (c. 1925-40), and what did it try to be?
notes.back: Modern and ornamental: machine-age geometry (zigzags, chevrons, sunbursts, stepped forms) in luxury materials, named after the 1925 Paris Exposition. Glamour for cinemas, skyscrapers, liners, radios.
notes.extra: Anchors: Chrysler Building (1930), Radio City Music Hall, Miami Beach hotels, Napier (NZ).

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: How do you recognise Art Deco on sight?
notes.back: Stepped silhouettes, vertical emphasis, stylised geometric ornament (sunrise fans, chevrons, zigzags), polished stone and metal, bold lettering; later Streamline Moderne adds rounded corners and horizontal speed lines.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: Art Nouveau vs Art Deco: how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: Art Nouveau (1890s-1910): organic, asymmetric, flowing curves, handmade. Art Deco (1920s-30s): geometric, symmetric, angular, machine-inspired, mass-produced glamour.
notes.analogy: Nouveau is a vine; Deco is a sunburst.

notes.deck: Architecture Styles::08 Skyscraper, Art Nouveau, Arts & Crafts, Art Deco
notes.front: What is Streamline Moderne?
notes.back: The late-1930s offshoot of Art Deco: smooth curved corners, horizontal bands, porthole windows, chrome and glass block, borrowed from ships, trains and aerodynamics. Diners, bus stations, Miami hotels.

notes.front: What did Modernism reject, and what did it let form follow from?
notes.back: It rejected historical styles and applied ornament. Form was to come from function, structure and new materials (steel, concrete, glass).

notes.front: What attitude to the machine and to society defined Modernism?
notes.back: Embrace the machine and industrial production, and use design to reform society: light, air and housing for all.

notes.text: Modernism's immediate forerunners: {{c1::Auguste Perret}} showed reinforced concrete as architecture (Rue Franklin flats, 1903); {{c2::Peter Behrens}} gave industry a monumental face (AEG Turbine Factory, 1909) and employed Gropius, Mies and Le Corbusier; the {{c3::Deutscher Werkbund}} (1907) linked designers with manufacturers.

notes.front: What was the Bauhaus, and why does its name stand for modernism?
notes.back: The school Gropius founded at Weimar in 1919 (moved to Dessau 1925, closed by the Nazis 1933) to unite art, craft and industrial production. Its teachers and students emigrated and spread the approach worldwide.
notes.extra: People: Gropius, Mies (last director), Kandinsky, Klee, Breuer, Albers. Gropius and Breuer went to Harvard, Mies to Chicago.

notes.front: What does the Bauhaus building at Dessau (1926) show about modernist composition?
notes.back: Asymmetric wings organised by function (workshops, studios, school), a glass curtain wall across the workshop block, flat roofs, white render, no ornament, no main facade: you must walk around it.

notes.front: What is Le Corbusier's Dom-ino idea (1914)?
notes.back: A diagram: flat concrete slabs on six slim columns with a free-standing stair. Structure reduced to a skeleton, so walls, windows and plan become free. The seed of the five points.
notes.analogy: A bookshelf with no back or sides: you can put anything on the shelves.

notes.front: How do the free plan and the free facade both follow from Le Corbusier's Dom-ino skeleton?
notes.back: Slabs on slim columns carry all the load, so interior partitions bear nothing and can go anywhere (free plan), and the exterior walls bear nothing either (free facade).

notes.text: Le Corbusier's five points (1927): {{c1::pilotis}} lift the house off the ground; a {{c2::roof garden}} replaces the lost ground; the {{c3::free plan}} puts partitions anywhere; {{c4::ribbon windows}} run horizontally; the {{c5::free facade}} is a non-bearing skin.
notes.extra: Root: all five follow from the concrete frame carrying the load instead of walls. Anchor: Villa Savoye, Poissy (1931).

notes.front: What did Le Corbusier mean by a house as a 'machine for living in'?
notes.back: Houses should be designed as rigorously as ocean liners, cars and aircraft: from needs, efficiency and mass production, not from tradition. Not that homes should feel mechanical, but that they should be engineered.

notes.front: Why does Le Corbusier appear in both the white International Style and raw Brutalism?
notes.back: His pre-war villas were smooth white machines; after 1945 he used unfinished board-marked concrete (béton brut) at the Unité d'Habitation (1952), Ronchamp and Chandigarh. Same man, two eras, two materials.

notes.front: What are the signature ideas of Mies van der Rohe?
notes.back: 'Less is more': structure as the only expression, flowing space defined by free-standing planes, steel and glass with exquisite proportions and details ('God is in the details').
notes.extra: Anchors: Barcelona Pavilion (1929), Farnsworth House (1951), Seagram Building (1958), IIT campus, Neue Nationalgalerie.

notes.front: What is the small irony in the Seagram Building's bronze I-beams?
notes.back: The vertical I-sections on the facade are not the structure (fire code buried the real steel in concrete); they are applied to express structure. Even Mies ornamented, with the image of structure.

notes.text: Hitchcock and Johnson's 1932 MoMA show named the International Style by three principles: architecture as {{c1::volume}} (thin skin over a skeleton) rather than mass; {{c2::regularity}} (the grid) rather than axial symmetry; and {{c3::no applied ornament}}.

notes.front: How do you recognise the International Style on sight?
notes.back: White or glass rectangular volumes, flat roofs, ribbon or curtain-wall windows, no cornice or base, pilotis, asymmetric but regular composition, no decoration; looks the same in any country (hence the name).
notes.analogy: Volume not mass: a balloon, not a boulder.

notes.front: What was De Stijl's contribution to architecture?
notes.back: Buildings as compositions of sliding rectangular planes and lines in primary colours, white, grey and black: Rietveld's Schröder House (1924). Space as a Mondrian in three dimensions; it influenced Mies's Barcelona Pavilion.

notes.front: What was Frank Lloyd Wright's 'organic architecture'?
notes.back: Building grown from its site, materials and the life inside, as a unified whole rather than a box with rooms: low horizontal lines, the hearth as core, open flowing plan, natural materials, long overhanging eaves.
notes.analogy: A building that grows from the site like a tree rather than landing on it like a spaceship.
notes.extra: Anchors: Robie House (Prairie, 1910), Fallingwater (1937), Johnson Wax (1939), Guggenheim (1959), the Usonian houses.

notes.front: How do you recognise a Prairie School house?
notes.back: Strong horizontals: low hipped roofs with huge overhangs, bands of casement windows, brick courses emphasised, a massive central chimney, no attic or basement; it looks pressed against the flat prairie.

notes.front: Wright vs European modernism: how did they differ?
notes.back: Wright: site-specific, natural materials, warm earth tones, horizontal, the house as shelter rooted in nature. Europeans: universal, white, machine-like, lifted off the ground on pilotis. Wright called the International Style 'flat-chested'.

notes.front: What makes Fallingwater (1937) a structural statement?
notes.back: Reinforced-concrete terraces cantilever over a waterfall from a stone core anchored in the rock. It uses modernism's material to make the opposite point: not a machine but a building growing out of a cliff.
notes.extra: Footnote: the cantilevers sagged for decades and were post-tensioned in 2002; Wright had under-reinforced them.

notes.front: What did Alvar Aalto add to modernism?
notes.back: A humanised Nordic version: curved forms, wood, brick, warm light, attention to the hand and the body (Paimio Sanatorium, Villa Mairea, Säynätsalo). Proof modernism need not be hard and white.

notes.front: What was CIAM's Athens Charter (1933), and what went wrong with it?
notes.back: The 'functional city': separate zones for living, working, recreation and traffic; housing in tall slabs in green space. Applied to post-war reconstruction it produced monotonous estates and dead streets; Jane Jacobs and Team 10 attacked it.
notes.analogy: Sorting a city like a filing cabinet, one drawer per function; nobody wants to live in a filing cabinet.

notes.front: Why is the demolition of Pruitt-Igoe (St Louis, 1972) a landmark?
notes.back: A modernist housing project of 33 slabs, finished 1956 and dynamited 16 years later after social collapse. Jencks dated 'the death of modern architecture' to it; postmodernism used it as proof that design cannot fix society by itself.

notes.front: Why did modernism insist on the flat roof, and what was the cost?
notes.back: It expressed the slab, rejected the traditional 'house' silhouette and gave a usable roof terrace. Early membranes leaked and stained the white walls; many famous villas were lawsuits waiting to happen.

notes.front: What did Louis Kahn bring back into modernism?
notes.back: Monumentality, mass and ancient geometry: 'served and servant spaces' (separating rooms from ducts and stairs), brick and concrete left honest, light as material. A bridge from the International Style to Brutalism and beyond.
notes.analogy: A restaurant: front of house and back of house each get their own rooms, and you can tell which is which.
notes.extra: Anchors: Salk Institute (1965), Kimbell Art Museum (1972), National Assembly Dhaka (1982).

notes.front: What was Expressionist architecture (c. 1910-25)?
notes.back: A short-lived German/Dutch strand that treated buildings as sculpted emotion: Mendelsohn's streamlined Einstein Tower (1921), Poelzig's cave-like Grosses Schauspielhaus, Amsterdam School brick. The ancestor of Ronchamp, Saarinen and Gehry.

notes.front: What is Brutalism, and where does the name come from?
notes.back: Post-war architecture (c. 1950-75) in raw exposed concrete (béton brut), massive sculptural forms, structure and services shown as found. Named by the Smithsons (New Brutalism, 1953) and Banham; the 'brutal' pun stuck.
notes.analogy: Concrete with the formwork's fingerprints left on: the building shows how it was made.
notes.extra: Anchors: Unité d'Habitation, Marseille; Boston City Hall; Barbican; Trellick Tower; Habitat 67; Chandigarh; Yale Art and Architecture.

notes.front: How do you recognise Brutalism on sight?
notes.back: Unfinished concrete with the timber formwork grain visible, heavy cantilevered blocks, repetitive modules, deep window recesses, exposed service towers and walkways, monumental weight, often set on a podium.

notes.front: What was Brutalism's ethic (as opposed to its look)?
notes.back: Honesty: show materials as they are, structure as it works, services where they run; dignity for public programmes (housing, universities, civic halls). Banham: 'an ethic, not an aesthetic'.

notes.front: Why did Brutalism fall from favour, and why is it revalued now?
notes.back: Concrete weathers badly in wet climates, maintenance was starved, and the buildings housed failing public programmes, so they became symbols of decline. Revalued since the 2010s for sculptural ambition, generosity and solidity.

notes.front: International Style vs Brutalism: how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: International Style: light, thin, smooth, white or glass, floating on pilotis. Brutalism: heavy, rough, grey, sculptural masses that sit on the ground. Both share no ornament and honest structure.

notes.front: What was Japanese Metabolism (1960s)?
notes.back: Buildings as growing organisms: permanent megastructure cores with plug-in replaceable capsules (Kurokawa's Nakagin Capsule Tower, 1972, demolished 2022). Few capsules were ever replaced; the metaphor outran the practice.

notes.front: What did Postmodernism react against, and what did it propose?
notes.back: Against modernism's blank abstraction and contempt for history and ordinary taste. For: historical references, symbolism, colour, irony and context. Venturi: 'Less is a bore' (Complexity and Contradiction, 1966).
notes.analogy: Architecture with air quotes.

notes.front: How do you recognise Postmodern architecture on sight?
notes.back: Classical motifs (columns, keystones, pediments) oversized, flattened or in the wrong material, bright colours and pastel, playful tops on towers, split and broken pediments used as jokes, collage of styles.
notes.extra: Anchors: Johnson's AT&T Building with its Chippendale top (1984), Graves's Portland Building, Moore's Piazza d'Italia, Stirling's Neue Staatsgalerie, Venturi's Vanna Venturi House.

notes.front: What is 'duck' vs 'decorated shed' (Venturi, Scott Brown, 1972)?
notes.back: A duck is a building whose whole form is the symbol (the duck-shaped duck stand, or a modernist building contorted to express function). A decorated shed is a plain box with signs and ornament applied. They argued the shed is more honest and cheaper.
notes.analogy: A sign-shaped building versus a building with a sign on it.

notes.front: What is the Vanna Venturi House (1964) saying?
notes.back: A house that looks like a child's drawing of a house (gable, chimney) but with the gable split, a non-centred door and an applied arch: 'a building is both ordinary and complex'. The opening shot of postmodernism.

notes.front: What is Aldo Rossi's idea of typology, and how is it postmodern?
notes.back: Cities carry persistent building types (courtyard, arcade, tower) with collective memory; new buildings should work with these forms rather than invent from function. A sober European postmodernism, no jokes.
notes.source: Rossi · The Architecture of the City 1966

notes.front: What is New Urbanism, and what does it react against?
notes.back: A 1980s-on movement (Duany, Plater-Zyberk; Seaside, Florida) reviving walkable, mixed-use, traditional-looking neighbourhoods with streets, squares and porches, against car-dependent sprawl and zoning by function.
notes.extra: Critique: often accused of nostalgia and stage-set styling; the planning ideas have outlived the styling.

notes.front: What is High-tech architecture?
notes.back: Structure, services and circulation turned inside-out and celebrated: exposed steel, ducts, escalators and tension cables, often colour-coded, leaving flexible open floors inside. Engineering (Arup, Rice) as the aesthetic.
notes.analogy: A watch with a transparent back: the mechanism is the decoration.
notes.extra: Anchors: Centre Pompidou (Piano and Rogers, 1977), Lloyd's of London (Rogers, 1986), HSBC Hong Kong (Foster, 1985), Grimshaw's Waterloo terminal.

notes.front: What is High-tech's lineage, and what did it react against?
notes.back: Heirs of Paxton, Eiffel and the train shed, plus Buckminster Fuller. They rejected postmodernism's historical costume as dishonest and Brutalism's heaviness; the future, not the past, was the reference.

notes.front: Brutalism vs High-tech: both show their structure; how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: Brutalism: heavy cast concrete, mass, monumentality, few parts. High-tech: light bolted steel, cables, glass, many articulated components, machine imagery, bright colour.

notes.front: What is Deconstructivism?
notes.back: Architecture of fragmentation and instability from the late 1980s: tilted walls, colliding volumes, non-rectilinear geometry, apparently random order. Named by the 1988 MoMA show (Johnson and Wigley), loosely citing Derrida and Russian Constructivism.
notes.analogy: A building photographed mid-explosion.
notes.extra: Anchors: Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao (1997), Libeskind's Jewish Museum Berlin, Hadid's Vitra Fire Station, Eisenman's Wexner Center, Tschumi's Parc de la Villette, Coop Himmelb(l)au.

notes.front: How do you recognise Deconstructivism on sight?
notes.back: Nothing looks plumb: skewed walls, fractured surfaces, shards and warped metal cladding, volumes that seem to crash into each other, no readable base-middle-top. It looks unfinished or exploded on purpose.

notes.front: Postmodernism vs Deconstructivism: how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: Postmodernism quotes history with a wink: columns, pediments, colour, symmetry subverted. Deconstructivism quotes nothing: abstract fragmented geometry, no historical motif, disorder as the theme.

notes.front: What made Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao (1997) technically possible, and what is the 'Bilbao effect'?
notes.back: Aerospace software (CATIA) translated his sculptural models into buildable titanium panels and steel. The museum revived a rust-belt city's image, so cities worldwide commissioned 'iconic' buildings expecting the same.
notes.extra: Caveat: most copies did not work; Bilbao also had a metro, a port clean-up and a decade of investment.

notes.front: What is critical regionalism (Frampton, 1983)?
