notes.back: A middle path: modern construction and abstraction, but rooted in local climate, light, topography and craft, resisting both placeless modernism and postmodern scenography.
notes.extra: Anchors: Barragán (Mexico, coloured walls), Siza (Portugal), Ando (Japan), Utzon, Murcutt (Australia).

notes.front: What is Tadao Ando's signature, and why does it count as regional?
notes.back: Silky, precisely cast concrete walls with formwork tie-holes, geometry and silence, light cut through slots (Church of the Light, 1989). Japanese spatial restraint and craft perfection in a Western material.

notes.front: What is parametricism?
notes.back: Design where form is generated by algorithms and parameters (sun, flow, structure, script) rather than drawn, giving continuous curved surfaces and non-repeating components. Named by Patrik Schumacher (2008) as the style of the digital age.
notes.analogy: Form as the output of a spreadsheet: change an input and the whole building reflows.
notes.extra: Anchors: Hadid's Heydar Aliyev Center (Baku, 2012), Galaxy SOHO; Foster's Gherkin exterior grid.

notes.front: What did digital fabrication change about building?
notes.back: Mass customisation: once a machine cuts each panel from a model, a thousand different parts cost about the same as a thousand identical ones. Repetition, modernism's economic law, stopped being mandatory.
notes.analogy: A printer does not care whether every page is the same.

notes.front: What is BIM, and why does it matter beyond drawing?
notes.back: Building Information Modelling: one shared 3D model carrying geometry, materials, cost and schedule, from which drawings are views. It shifts the architect's output from drawings to a database other disciplines also edit.

notes.front: Why is sustainability now the central driver of architectural debate?
notes.back: Buildings account for roughly 35-40% of energy-related CO2 (operation plus construction). No climate target is reachable without changing how buildings are heated, cooled, built and reused.

notes.front: Operational vs embodied carbon: what is the difference, and why has attention shifted?
notes.back: Operational: emissions from running the building (heating, lighting). Embodied: emissions from making its materials and building it (cement, steel). As operations decarbonise, embodied carbon becomes the larger share, favouring reuse and timber.
notes.analogy: Sticker price vs running cost of a car: once the car is electric, the sticker is where the carbon is.

notes.text: Passive design uses the building itself before any machine: {{c1::orientation}} to catch winter sun, {{c2::shading}} (overhangs) to block summer sun, {{c3::thermal mass}} to store heat, high {{c4::insulation and airtightness}}, and {{c5::cross or stack ventilation}} for cooling.

notes.front: Why does a roof overhang do double duty on a south-facing window?
notes.back: The summer sun is high, so the overhang shades the glass; the winter sun is low, so it passes under and warms the floor slab. Geometry alone switches between cooling and heating modes.

notes.front: What is the Passivhaus standard?
notes.back: A performance standard (Germany, 1991): heating demand ≤ 15 kWh/m² per year, airtightness ≤ 0.6 air changes per hour at 50 Pa, achieved with super-insulation, triple glazing, no thermal bridges and heat-recovery ventilation.
notes.analogy: A thermos flask: so well sealed and insulated that body heat and the sun keep it warm.

notes.front: LEED / BREEAM vs Passivhaus: what kind of thing is each?
notes.back: LEED and BREEAM are broad points-based rating schemes (energy, water, site, materials, indoor quality) with medal levels. Passivhaus is a narrow, strict physics standard for energy and comfort. A building can have one without the other.

notes.front: What is mass timber, and why is it the material story of the 2010s-20s?
notes.back: Engineered wood (CLT panels, glulam beams) strong enough for mid- and high-rise frames. It stores carbon instead of emitting it like cement and steel, is light, prefabricated and fast to erect.
notes.extra: Anchors: Mjøstårnet, Norway (85 m, 2019); Ascent, Milwaukee (87 m, 2022); Sara Kulturhus, Skellefteå.

notes.front: CLT vs glulam: what is the difference?
notes.back: CLT (cross-laminated timber): boards glued in alternating 90° layers into large panels for walls and floors. Glulam: boards glued parallel into long beams and columns. CLT is the plate, glulam the stick.

notes.front: How does mass timber handle fire?
notes.back: A thick timber element chars on the outside at a predictable rate (~0.7 mm/min) and the char layer insulates the core, so it keeps carrying load for a calculable time. Codes size members with a sacrificial char layer.
notes.analogy: A thick log in a fireplace burns slowly from the outside; kindling is what burns fast.

notes.front: Why is adaptive reuse now preferred over demolition?
notes.back: The existing structure's embodied carbon is already spent; keeping it avoids new concrete and steel, saves time and keeps urban memory. Tate Modern (power station, 2000) and the High Line (rail viaduct, 2009) made it fashionable.
notes.extra: Slogan: 'the greenest building is the one already built.' Lacaton & Vassal (Pritzker 2021): 'never demolish'.

notes.front: What structural idea let towers pass ~400 m, and who introduced it?
notes.back: Fazlur Khan's tube (1960s): the perimeter acts as a hollow stiff tube resisting wind, instead of a core alone. Bundled tubes (Sears/Willis Tower), braced tubes (John Hancock), later buttressed cores (Burj Khalifa, 828 m).
notes.analogy: A bamboo stalk: hollow yet stiff, because the strength sits at the perimeter.

notes.front: Why is a perimeter tube stiffer against wind than a central core using the same amount of material?
notes.back: Bending resistance grows with how far material sits from the centre line. Putting the material in the outer wall gives it a long lever arm against wind, which a core alone cannot match.

notes.front: What does a tuned mass damper do in a skyscraper?
notes.back: A huge pendulum mass near the top swings out of phase with the building's wind sway, cancelling most of the motion for the comfort of occupants. Taipei 101's 660-tonne gold sphere is the famous one.
notes.analogy: A heavy pendulum that leans the other way every time the tower leans.

notes.front: What is a diagrid, and what does it let a facade do?
notes.back: A diagonal grid of steel members that is both structure and facade, carrying gravity and wind together, so no vertical columns are needed at the perimeter. Foster's Gherkin (2004), Hearst Tower (2006).
notes.analogy: Chain-link fencing that holds the building up.

notes.front: What is biophilic design, and what is the evidence behind it?
notes.back: Bringing nature into buildings: daylight, views, plants, natural materials and patterns. Studies link it to faster recovery in hospitals (Ulrich, 1984), better concentration and lower stress; green facades are its visible sign (Bosco Verticale, Milan).

notes.front: What is design for disassembly (circular architecture)?
notes.back: Building so components can be taken apart and reused: bolted not welded, dry joints not glue, material passports recording what is where. Treats the building as a temporary store of materials rather than future rubble.

notes.front: What does Francis Kéré (Pritzker 2022) represent in contemporary architecture?
notes.back: The return of vernacular logic with modern intelligence: local clay bricks, community-built, double roofs that ventilate without electricity (Gando school, Burkina Faso). Sustainability as climate and culture, not gadgets.

notes.front: What is 'starchitecture', and what is the main critique?
notes.back: Iconic signature buildings by global brand-name architects commissioned for prestige and marketing. Critics: they ignore context, cost and use, and treat cities as a collection of logos rather than fabric.

notes.front: What is architectural minimalism, and how does it differ from the International Style?
notes.back: Reduction to essentials with intense attention to material, light and proportion (Zumthor's Therme Vals, Pawson, Ando). Unlike the machine-made white box, it is sensuous and craft-heavy: expensive simplicity.

notes.text: Reading any building in three questions: what {{c1::structural idea}} makes it stand (wall, arch, frame, shell); what it {{c2::reacted against}} (the previous style's excess or blankness); and what on the facade {{c3::gives the style away}} (arch shape, ornament, roof, material).
